21, 2025, in Sacramento, California. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images/TNS) Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America/TNS Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Gov.

Gavin Newsom on Friday ordered the formation of a panel to come up with safety regulations for the state’s artificial intelligence companies, including the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that go rogue.

Newsom issued an executive order to convene “a group of world-leading experts” to provide a “guide” for the state to bolster its laws around AI security, according to a statement from the governor’s office.
The panel could consider proposals for independent third parties to write safety plans or for companies to develop an emergency shutoff.
Newsom, who is considering a 2028 run for president, two years ago vetoed a state bill that would have mandated a kill switch.

Some Democratic and Republican leaders around the country are scrambling to come up with safety proposals after employees at AI companies recently warned that the technology could create catastrophe, including ending humanity.

A researcher for AI company Anthropic said he left the company over concerns that AI companies, including OpenAI, are “gambling with our lives” as they race ahead to improve AI that could surpass human intelligence.
The researcher, Jacob Coxon, said in a social media post: “People building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” State Sen.
Christopher Cabaldon, a West Sacramento Democrat who chairs the state committee overseeing technology issues, told the Los Angeles Times he’ll hold hearings on artificial intelligence this fall.
Those meetings were planned before the recent warnings about AI’s dangers, but will be informed by the events of the last few weeks, he said.
Any new laws could have a disproportionate effect on the global tech industry because many top AI companies are based in California.

AI expert Geoffrey Hinton, who won a Nobel Prize in 2024 for his work on machine learning, expressed doubt on CNN this week that a “kill switch” would be effective since AI would “persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull the switch.” The risk, he said, is “AI itself getting much more intelligent and taking over.” A proposed law in 2024 by state Sen.
Scott Wiener, a San Francisco Democrat, would have required tech firms to be able to turn off the AI models they directly control if things go awry.
I want to maintain our innovation,” Newsom said at a Salesforce conference on AI in 2024.

Gavin Newsom wants a panel to develop safety regulations for California's artificial intelligence companies. (Juliana Yamada / Associated Press) California Gov.

Gavin Newsom on Friday became the latest politician to push for stronger artificial intelligence regulations following claims from AI experts that the technology could lead to widespread death and destruction.
Newsom issued an executive order for the creation of a panel to recommend safety rules, including the development of a possible "kill switch" for AI programs that go rogue.
It was a striking turn for the governor, who two years ago vetoed a bill that would have required AI companies to develop such a switch.
Josh Shapiro made a similar plea for AI safeguards , including third-party oversight and greater transparency.

Some Democratic and Republican leaders around the country are scrambling to come up with regulations after employees at AI companies recently warned that the technology could create catastrophe, including the end of humanity.
Lieu (D-Torrance) and Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) introduced a bill in July that would have required developers to have the capability to shut down powerful AI systems.
Tech companies deal with a patchwork of rules across different states and countries.
Executives including Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, who has close ties to Trump, have said publicly that no new regulation is needed.
Instead, they argue that company leaders should hold themselves accountable as an industry and not release unsafe products.

Advertisement Advertisement A researcher for AI company Anthropic said earlier this month that he left the firm over concerns that AI companies, including OpenAI, for whom he also worked, are "gambling with our lives" as they race ahead to improve AI that could surpass human intelligence.
The researcher, Jacob Coxon, said in a social media post: "People building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." State Sen.
Christopher Cabaldon (D-West Sacramento), who chairs the state committee overseeing technology issues, told The Times he'll hold hearings on artificial intelligence this fall.
There are still questions about how a kill switch would work.

In a video about the executive order, Newsom said an AI kill switch "means a lot of things depending on who you talk to." "We want to flesh out exactly what that means and how to come up with a framework that works," he said.

AI expert Geoffrey Hinton, who won a Nobel Prize in 2024 for his work on machine learning, expressed doubt on CNN this week that a kill switch would be effective since AI would "persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull the switch." The risk, he said, is "AI itself getting much more intelligent and taking over." Advertisement Advertisement A proposed law in 2024 by state Sen.
Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco) would have required tech firms to be able to turn off the AI models they directly control if things go awry.
